questions.q: What is a liberty of a Go group?
options: Any empty point on the board
A diagonal neighbour of a stone
An empty point orthogonally adjacent to any stone in the group
questions.why: A group is a maximal set of same-coloured stones connected orthogonally. It is captured when its last liberty is filled.

questions.q: How do you find a group and its liberties?
options: Count all stones of that colour
Flood fill from a stone through orthogonal same-colour neighbours, collecting empty neighbours as liberties
Check the four corners of the board
questions.why: BFS or DFS with a visited set. Liberties should be a set, since one empty point can border several stones of the group.

questions.q: A move fills the last liberty of an opponent group and also of the player's own group. What happens under standard rules?
options: The opponent group is captured first, which gives the player's group liberties, so the move is legal
questions.why: Captures of opposing stones are resolved before checking whether the moved stone's group has liberties.

questions.q: What does the positional superko rule forbid?
options: Any move that recreates a whole-board position that occurred earlier in the game
questions.why: This prevents endless cycles. Implementations usually keep a set of position hashes, such as Zobrist hashes.

questions.q: Under Tromp-Taylor area scoring, what does a player's score count?
options: Their stones on the board plus empty points that reach only their colour
questions.why: An empty region bordering both colours counts for neither. Komi is then added to White's score.

questions.q: What does komi compensate for?
questions.why: Values around 7.5 are common under area scoring. The half point prevents draws.

questions.q: Which moves should a legal-action mask mark as illegal?
options: Every point next to an opponent stone
Occupied points, suicides and superko violations; pass is always legal
questions.why: The policy head's output is masked before the softmax so illegal moves get zero probability.

questions.q: When does a Go game end in the usual self-play implementation?
options: When one player has no stones
After two consecutive passes, or at a move limit
questions.why: The final position is then scored, giving +1 or -1 as the value target.

questions.q: What does the AlphaGo Zero input encoding include?
options: Several planes of recent board history for each player plus a plane for the colour to move
Only the current board as a single plane
questions.why: History planes capture information such as recent captures and ko, which aren't visible from the current position alone.

questions.q: Why does the input include a plane for whose turn it is?
options: The same stones can be good for one player and bad for the other; also komi favours White
questions.why: Positions are often encoded from the current player's perspective, and the colour plane resolves the remaining asymmetry.

questions.q: What is the structure of an AlphaGo Zero residual block?
options: Conv–BN–ReLU–conv–BN, add the skip connection, then ReLU
questions.why: The tower stacks many such blocks of 3×3 convolutions with 256 filters in the full model.

questions.q: What does the policy head output?
options: A probability (or logit) for each board point plus pass
questions.why: For 19×19 that is 362 outputs. It serves as the prior for tree search.

questions.q: What does the value head output?
options: A scalar in [-1, 1] estimating the expected outcome for the player to move
questions.why: A tanh output fits the ±1 game result.

questions.q: Why use one network with two heads instead of separate policy and value networks?
options: The shared tower learns features useful for both, and the combined training regularises it
It halves the number of outputs
Value and policy are the same thing
questions.why: AlphaGo Zero reported that the dual network improved playing strength over separate ones.

questions.q: What does batch normalisation do at inference time in these networks?
options: Uses stored running mean and variance, not batch statistics
questions.why: MCTS often evaluates single positions, so batch statistics would be meaningless.

questions.q: Why is the network fully convolutional before the heads?
options: Go patterns are local and translation-invariant to a degree, which convolutions exploit with few parameters
Fully connected layers can't be trained
questions.why: The 3×3 receptive field grows with depth until it covers the whole board.

questions.q: What statistics does each MCTS edge (s, a) store?
options: Visit count N, total value W, mean value Q and prior P
The full game tree below it
questions.why: Q = W/N. The prior P comes from the network when the node is expanded.

questions.q: What does the PUCT selection rule choose?
options: The action with the highest prior only
questions.why: The second term favours actions the network likes and that haven't been explored much. It shrinks as visits grow.

questions.q: How should an unvisited edge's Q be set?
options: To a fixed default such as 0 (or a parent-based estimate), chosen consistently
questions.why: Implementations differ. The choice affects how aggressively unvisited moves are tried.

questions.q: What happens when a simulation reaches a leaf?
options: A random rollout to the end of the game is played
The search restarts at the root
The network evaluates it, giving priors for its children and a value to back up
questions.why: AlphaGo Zero dropped rollouts entirely and relied on the value head.

questions.q: During backup, why is the value's sign flipped at each level?
options: Players alternate, so a good position for one player is bad for the other
questions.why: Each edge's Q is stored from the perspective of the player choosing that action.

questions.q: Why must illegal moves get zero prior at expansion?
options: The network never assigns them probability
They are legal in the tree
So the search never selects them, and the remaining priors are renormalised to sum to 1
questions.why: Mask and renormalise before storing priors.

questions.q: What does "virtual loss" do in parallel MCTS?
options: Temporarily lowers a path's value while a simulation is in flight, so other threads explore different paths
questions.why: It is undone when the real value is backed up.

questions.q: Why might a deterministic MCTS implementation be useful for testing?
options: Fixed tie-breaking and no random noise give reproducible visit counts that can be compared exactly
It is the only correct version
questions.why: Break ties by lowest action index and turn off Dirichlet noise for tests.

questions.q: Why is Dirichlet noise added to the root priors during self-play?
options: To make sure every move at the root gets some exploration, even ones the network currently dislikes
questions.why: The mix is $(1-\epsilon)P + \epsilon\,\eta$ with η ~ Dir(α). AlphaGo Zero used ε = 0.25 and α = 0.03 for 19×19.

questions.q: Why is the Dirichlet α smaller for larger boards?
options: It is larger for larger boards
There are more legal moves, so a small α concentrates noise on a few moves instead of spreading it thinly
questions.why: α is often set around 10 divided by the typical number of legal moves.

questions.q: How is the training policy target built from a search?
options: The root visit counts raised to the power 1/τ and normalised
The Q-values passed through a softmax
A one-hot of the move played, always
questions.why: With τ = 1 it is proportional to visits; as τ → 0 it approaches a one-hot of the most visited move.

questions.q: Why is temperature τ = 1 used for the first moves and τ → 0 afterwards?
options: It is required by the rules
Early randomness gives diverse openings for training; later moves are played as strongly as possible
Because the network is untrained early
questions.why: AlphaGo Zero used τ = 1 for the first 30 moves of each self-play game.

questions.q: What is the AlphaGo Zero loss?
questions.why: z is the game outcome from the player's perspective, π the search policy, and the last term is L2 regularisation.

questions.q: What is the value target z for a position?
options: The final game result (+1 or -1) from the perspective of the player to move in that position
questions.why: Every position in a game gets the same outcome, with the sign set by whose turn it was.

questions.q: Why is the search policy a better training target than the raw network policy?
options: Search improves on the prior by looking ahead, so training on it is a form of policy improvement
questions.why: MCTS acts as a policy improvement operator; the network distils the improved policy.

questions.q: Why should positions near the end of a resigned game be handled carefully?
options: False resignations give wrong outcome labels; a fraction of games are played out to check the resignation threshold
questions.why: AlphaGo Zero disabled resignation in 10% of games to keep the false-positive rate below 5%.

questions.q: Why sample training batches from a window of recent self-play games?
options: Older games come from weaker networks; a window keeps data fairly current while still mixing many games
It removes the need for shuffling
questions.why: AlphaGo Zero sampled from the most recent 500,000 games.

questions.q: Why sample positions uniformly across games rather than taking whole games?
options: Uniform sampling is required by the loss
Whole games don't fit in memory
Positions within one game are highly correlated, which would bias each batch
questions.why: Mixing positions from many games makes batches closer to independent samples.

questions.q: How many symmetries does a square Go board have?
options: 8 (four rotations, each with or without reflection)
questions.why: This is the dihedral group of the square. Komi and the rules are invariant under all of them.

questions.q: When applying a symmetry to a training example, what must be transformed?
options: Both the input planes and the policy target, with pass left unchanged
questions.why: Transforming only the input would teach the network to play mirrored moves.

questions.q: How can symmetry be used at evaluation time?
options: Evaluate a randomly transformed position and map the policy back, or average over several transforms
questions.why: Random transforms reduce bias from any asymmetry the network has learned.

questions.q: In one training step for the dual-head network, how are the two losses combined?
options: Only the policy loss is backpropagated
Summed (with the L2 term), and one backward pass updates the shared tower and both heads
Two separate optimisers on separate towers
The value loss is computed but not used
questions.why: AlphaGo Zero weighted the two terms equally.

questions.q: How did AlphaGo Zero decide whether a newly trained network replaced the current self-play network?
options: The new network had to win at least 55% of evaluation games against it
When its loss went below a threshold
After a fixed number of steps
questions.why: AlphaZero later dropped this gating and always used the latest network.

questions.q: What does the whole loop alternate between?
options: Self-play with MCTS to make data, and training the network on that data
Supervised learning on human games only
questions.why: Better networks make better searches, which make better training targets.
